newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani state airline plans cost cuts.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani state airline plans cost cuts.

text.p: The state-run Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), faced with declining profits, says it plans to cut operational expenses and improve services to boost revenues.
"There are many reasons for declining profits," PIA chairman Shahid Khaqan Abbasi told Reuters in an interview.

"The operational costs have soared because of an ageing fleet, surplus staff, corruption, leakages and 50 percent increase in fuel rates over last two years. But fare-structure remained unchanged," he said.

PIA's profits have been falling in recent years. Its after-tax profit plunged to 65 million rupees ($1.6 million) in fiscal 1995/96 (July/June) from 293 million in the previous year. In the first half of fiscal 1996/97 to December, its profit dipped to 22.303 million compared to 182.540 million in the year-ago period.

PIA has closed down several non-profitable international routes, including those to Beirut, Washington and Athens, and plans to cut the number of flights on several others in a bid to cut operational costs.

"Our revenues haven't kept pace even with inflation, which remained at around 10 percent during the last few years," Abbasi said. "Devaluation of the rupee also hit us hard because most of our expenses are in foreign currency."
NON-PROFITABLE ROUTES
Now PIA is rationalising its route structure by shutting traditionally non-profitable routes and opening new ones, including those to Hong Kong, South Africa and Australia.
"PIA can increase revenues by offering a better product and good service," Abbasi said. "Today we are not competitive and have to shun our government bureaucracy style."
He said PIA would concentrate on its core activity of transporting passengers and cargo and would gradually wind up its support services.
The airline also runs hospitals, poultry farms, hotels, flight kitchen, ground support operations, training centres, planetariums, sports departments and plant nurseries which add to its expenses.
SURPLUS STAFF, CORRUPTION

Abbasi said salaries and perks of about 21,000 regular and 4,000 contractual PIA employees accounted for almost 28 percent of the airline's total expenses compared to the industry standards of 18 to 20 percent.
"We plan right-sizing the number of employees. In some places, staff is surplus and at others it is deficient. We have to shift people around," he said.
"Every year 600 to 800 people are retiring. We plan fewer replacements to achieve a certain balance. Action will also be taken against corrupt officials."
PIA officials say corruption and leakages account for about 15 percent of the airline's expenses.
FLEET MODERNISATION
Abbasi said PIA planned to modernise its fleet over the next three to five years at a cost of $1.5 billion.
"Fleet replacement is important. Almost every airline has new aeroplanes from five- to seven-year-old while we are competing with 20-year-old aeroplanes."
He said although these planes were absolutely safe, their operational cost was higher. "Other airlines have a mix of old and new (planes) in their fleet. PIA has also to do this."
PIA now has eight Boeing 747-200s, nine Airbus A300-B4s, six Airbus A310-300s, six Boeing 737-300s, two Boeing 707 cargo planes, 13 Fokker F-27s and two Twin Otters.
Abbasi said the fleet modernisation had already been started and in the next couple of years, PIA would retire six of its eight Boeing 747-200s and introduce new aircraft, he said.
"It's an ambitious plan. PIA will replace old Fokker planes, then old A-300s would be dumped and so would be the 737s."
PRIVATISATION DELAYED
Abbasi said privatisation was a cornerstone of the policy of Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government, but PIA was not on the priority list for this.
"It is not a matter of putting it off, but doing it at the right time. We want to make PIA efficent and are weighing options.

"Privatisation does not mean total sale. It may mean bringing in private management, a strategic investor, or privatising its subsidies or total outright sale of the airline or maybe a combination of a few of these... But we have not finalised yet."
"PIA performs a lot of functions which a private sector airline will not do. It has a role in overall national security programme. At least for the time being its privatisation is not a priority."
